items.title: Vulnerable Coronary Plaques on CT Angiography: Imaging Biomarkers, Artificial Intelligence, and Emerging Technologies for Risk Stratification
items.abstract: Background: Coronary artery disease remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Increasing evidence has demonstrated that many acute coronary events originate not from severely obstructive lesions but from structurally unstable atherosclerotic plaques. Consequently, the identification of vulnerable plaques has become a major objective in contemporary cardiovascular imaging. Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) has evolved from a modality primarily focused on luminal stenosis assessment into a comprehensive non-invasive technique capable of evaluating plaque morphology, composition, and overall coronary atherosclerotic burden. Results: Our review summarizes current evidence regarding the role of CCTA in the detection and characterization of vulnerable coronary plaques. Particular emphasis is placed on imaging biomarkers associated with plaque instability, including low-attenuation plaque, positive remodeling, spotty calcifications, and the napkin-ring sign, which have been consistently linked to an increased risk of adverse cardiovascular events. Advances in quantitative plaque analysis have further enhanced the ability of CCTA to assess plaque burden and monitor disease progression. Emerging technologies are rapidly expanding the capabilities of coronary CT imaging. Spectral CT techniques and photon-counting detector CT offer improved tissue characterization and enhanced visualization of plaque components. In parallel, artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms are enabling automated plaque detection, segmentation, and risk prediction, facilitating more precise and reproducible analysis of large imaging datasets. Conclusions: Despite these advances, limitations remain, including restricted spatial resolution for microstructural plaque assessment and the limited ability of conventional CT to directly evaluate biological processes such as inflammation. Future developments integrating advanced CT technologies, artificial intelligence, and multimodality imaging are expected to further improve the non-invasive identification of vulnerable plaques and personalized cardiovascular risk stratification.

items.title: We Need to talk about AI: Software in Modern Heliophysics
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing how scientific software is developed, used and maintained. This presentation explores what that means for heliophysics, where published results depend on layers of software and the communities that sustain them. It considers opportunities for AI to support research alongside questions about scientific validation, human understanding, environmental costs, bias and equitable access. Examples from open-source development highlight how easier code generation can shift effort towards reviewers and maintainers. Solar Orbiter provides a setting for examining the appeal of independent development and the longer-term benefits of shared software. The presentation concludes with approaches to funding and organising shared infrastructure, and asks how the heliophysics community can preserve responsibility, learning and collaboration as AI becomes part of everyday scientific work.

items.title: What are the Ethical Considerations to Keep in Mind When Integrating New Educational Technologies into the Classroom?: A Case Study of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: New educational technologies—such as artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI, and wearable monitoring devices—are profoundly reshaping classroom ecologies. While they drive greater precision, personalization, and efficiency in teaching and learning, they also give rise to multiple ethical dilemmas, including data privacy breaches, the entrenchment of algorithmic bias, the alienation of teacher-student relationships, the erosion of student agency, and the blurring of responsibility attribution. Grounded in the fundamental educational mission of "fostering virtue and cultivating persons," this paper dialectically examines four core ethical tensions arising from the integration of new educational technologies into the classroom: efficiency versus humanism, empowerment versus rights, fairness versus bias, and autonomy versus discipline. It systematically distills five overarching ethical principles—rights protection, fairness and justice, humanistic authenticity, agency cultivation, and shared responsibility—and proposes a practical pathway characterized by technology for good, ethics-first design, and multi-stakeholder governance. Finally, this paper provides a critical evaluation of the structural friction and feasibility limits of these principles, aiming to establish a robust moral foundation for the beneficial integration of technology and education within the global landscape.

items.title: What Do Borrower Workarounds Reveal? User-Derived Design Implications for Digital Finance in Indonesian Crowdlending
items.abstract: This study examines how Indonesian crowdlending borrowers navigate tensions among access, risk, and trust. It draws on interviews with 30 borrowersand uses an abductive, constructivist grounded-theory approach, with substantial intercoder reliability (Cohen’s kappa = 0.775). Four categories emerged: Paradoxical Necessity, Comparative Advantage Calculation, Risk-Exposure Management, and Institutional Legitimacy Navigation. Borrowers accommodate these tensions through temporal separation, cautious engagement, and legitimacy assessment. They preserve access by addressing immediate needs, comparing credit options, adjusting repayment practices after adverse experiences, and weighing regulatory status alongside platform terms and personal experience. Borrowers with longer or more adverse platform histories described more deliberate comparison, repayment management, and legitimacy assessment. However, the cross-sectional design cannot determine whether these differences reflect development over time or preexisting differences. Borrower workarounds indicate potential unmet design needs, especially in transparency, risk communication, and trust calibration, and provide borrower-derived implications for platform design and regulatory oversight.

items.title: When AI Education Moves Faster Than Teaching Practice: Teacher Labour Alienation in the Transitional Phase of AI Integration
items.abstract: Existing research on Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) has largely presupposed a mature landscape in which AI is fully embedded within schooling, whilst overlooking the initial transitional phase from conventional to AI-enabled instruction. Grounded in Marxist philosophy, this paper examines the central contradiction of this transitional period: namely, that social consciousness regarding the incorporation of AI into teaching has run considerably ahead of the material reality of instructional practice. From this disparity, three progressively intensified forms of alienation are derived: instructional performativity, wherein AI is reduced to a demonstration prop for open classes; the symbolic reification of AI, whereby it degenerates from a pedagogical aid into vacuous evaluative metrics; and reverse discipline over teachers by AI, such that quantifiable indicators come to serve as the primary measure of professional competence. Collectively, these three dimensions instantiate a Marxian cycle of alienation, characterised by a thoroughgoing estrangement from labour processes, labour products and species-being. The argument advanced here is that resolution of this crisis depends not upon further technological refinement, but rather upon restoring AI to its proper status as a productive force mediated by the historical agency of teachers themselves. Whilst the integration of AI into education presents a significant opportunity for pedagogical transformation, ultimate educational authority must remain vested in human practitioners. Focusing upon the alienation of teacher labour during this transitional moment, this study uncovers structural vulnerabilities latent within the AIED ecosystem via an analysis of these stratified alienated forms.

items.title: When AI Sounds Supportive: Comparing Conversational AI and Therapist Responses to Mental Health Disclosures
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives To compare artificial intelligence (AI) and therapist responses to real‐world mental health (MH) disclosures and evaluate differences in empathy, safety practices and contextual usefulness. Methods We analysed 937 unique MH disclosures and 2749 therapist responses using the Counsel Chat dataset. For each disclosure, we generated a standardised AI response using a large language model. Responses were evaluated across empathy, safety and contextual usefulness measures using automated metrics, blinded human ratings of 120 therapist‐AI response pairs, mixed effects regression models, and qualitative analyses of disagreement cases. Results AI responses scored higher than therapist responses on automated empathy ( β = 0.30; p < 0.001), human‐rated empathy ( β = 0.38; p < 0.001), emotional validation ( β = 0.40; p < 0.001) and automated safety ( β = 0.25; p < 0.001). AI safety advantages were largest for self‐harm or suicide‐related disclosures. Therapists scored higher on specificity/personalisation ( β = −0.62; p < 0.001) and helpfulness ( β = −0.23; p = 0.013); overall quality did not differ significantly. Conclusions As conversational AI becomes an increasingly common source of MH support, AI responses may offer strengths in empathic communication and explicit safety‐oriented guidance, whereas therapist responses were rated more highly for personalisation and contextual usefulness. These findings highlight different strengths across AI and therapist responses while underscoring the need for caution in interpreting response quality as clinical effectiveness. They also point to a potential role for conversational AI as an accessible first point of support within broader MH care systems, particularly where timely professional support is limited.

items.title: When AI Stops Being a Tool and Becomes an Actor
items.abstract: When AI Stops Being a Tool and Becomes an Actor examines what changes when artificial intelligence moves beyond responding to human instructions and begins independently planning, using tools, accessing systems, and taking actions on a user's behalf. The report brings together research across six disciplines—artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, philosophy, law, economics, and computing infrastructure—to examine the emerging consequences of agentic AI. It investigates the technical difference between chatbots and agents; the security risks created by memory, tool access, and external communication; the philosophical problem of responsibility and agency; emerging legal questions around authorization and liability; the economic implications of agents negotiating and transacting on behalf of humans; and the infrastructure changes accompanying an increasingly machine-mediated internet. Rather than treating agentic AI as inherently good or bad, the report examines what current evidence actually establishes, where uncertainty remains, and where the conclusions of different fields begin to diverge. The report's central finding is that no single human, system, or institution is currently positioned to trace where a given agentic decision actually came from. Agentic decision-making is distributed across model behavior, deployment choices, authorization structures, legal frameworks, and infrastructure. This report is an independent research publication by Lodestar and is based on peer-reviewed research, preprints, government and legal materials, and industry reporting available as of September 2026. Where evidence relies on a simulation, a single source, or an unreviewed preprint, the report identifies that uncertainty directly.

items.title: When the AI Self Becomes the Ideal Self: A Systematic Review of AI-Enhanced Self-Discrepancy, Appearance Anxiety, and Protective Psychological Factors
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) appearance technologies, including beauty filters, augmented reality (AR) modification and generative avatars, have individualized digital self-presentation. Unlike traditional media, these technologies create self-referential appearance ideals that create novel forms of self-discrepancy and appearance anxiety. A systematic review was conducted in peer-reviewed databases for empirical studies published from 2021 to 2026 that studied self-representation, self-discrepancy, appearance distress, and protective psychological constructs within this context of AI, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Emergent patterns were identified by using the narrative thematic synthesis method across eligible studies. A total of eight empirical studies were found that fulfilled the inclusion criteria. The themes that emerged were as follows: (1) AI-enhanced self as a novel appearance ideal of the self; (2) self-discrepancy as an operative mechanism between the appearance of idealized and non-idealized selves and psychological distress; (3) contextually related and protective moderators; and (4) representation modality—between aestheticizing versus non-aestheticizing appearance modalities and psychological distress. The findings from the synthesis showed that self-discrepancy, social self-comparison, and self-objectification are the three main routes for appearance anxiety. Theoretically, these non-idealizing avatars, high self-similarity, and goal-oriented use contexts were considered as protective buffers but were not consistently quantified. Most importantly, there was no empirical study that directly assessed positive body image constructs or body appreciation. The current research mainly focuses on the pathology aspect of AI appearance technology, and positive body image is not investigated. Empirical studies should be conducted in the future with the clear aim of examining if constructive, nonidealized relationships with the technologically enhanced body can foster psychological resilience, and if so, how.

items.title: Widening or Deepening? How Firms Integrate AI and Large Language Models into Research and Discovery
items.abstract: Multiple firms spanning expertise from material science and computational chemistry to pharmaceuticals have started investing into Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) to streamline and expedite their Research and Discovery (R&D) process; however, the effects of this newfound integration of AI into R&D remain unclear as it is yet to be understood whether it is changing how the process is conducted versus simply accelerating the process. This study utilizes qualitative data collected from seven semi-structured interviews with interviewees with expertise spanning from corporate research and startups to innovation economics in order to analyze the central question: does the integration of AI in R&D deepen research in already explored areas by accelerating it or does it widen the directions of research and introduce novel directions? Across all interviews, the most common limitation noted in AI’s integration in R&D was human validation. Regarding the central question, the results skewed towards the deepening trend. Many interviewees mentioned that the current usage of AI causes its integration to only accelerate and improve the discovery within research directions already explored; however, interviewees explained that this was a trend based on the methodology of R&D used by most firms rather than a technological barrier of the tool itself. These results suggest that firms and policymakers should thoroughly evaluate the productivity increase of AI rather than its potential and focus on solving the several bottlenecks still not tackled by AI: validation, human judgement, and physical experimentation.

items.title: Wings or shackles? Artificial intelligence and Chinese corporate internationalization
items.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence’s (AI) influence on corporate operations is receiving increasing social attention. Does AI significantly influence the international expansion of enterprises? Design/methodology/approach Based on theories such as multinational corporations, this study selects relevant data from Chinese-listed companies spanning the years 2011–2019, with a particular emphasis on how artificial intelligence directly influences the scope and degree of corporate internationalization. This study also considers the moderating effects of CEO information technology background (ITCEO), ESG performance and external regional environmental regulations. Findings The research results indicate that artificial intelligence improves the scope and degree of internationalization performance of enterprises. Heterogeneity analysis found that artificial intelligence has different impacts on state-owned enterprises and private enterprises. The CEO’s expertise in IT serves as a positive moderating factor, enhancing the direct correlation between artificial intelligence and the scope, as well as the degree of their company’s internationalization efforts. ESG performance serves as a positive moderating factor, enhancing the direct correlation between artificial intelligence and the scope of their company’s internationalization efforts. The external regional environmental regulations serve as a negative moderating factor. Originality/value This study innovatively integrates artificial intelligence (AI) into the analysis of both the scope and degree of enterprise internationalization, thereby enriching the literature on AI and its applications in business strategies. By incorporating AI, this research broadens the theoretical and empirical insights into the determinants affecting the scope and degree of corporate internationalization. This study systematically examines the moderating effects of CEOs with IT backgrounds, corporate ESG performance and regional environmental regulations, thereby extending the scope of research on the determinants of internationalization.

items.title: Workforce Strategies in the Age of AI: Designing Job Roles for A Post-Automation Economy
items.abstract: With the advancement in technology, the present process of business operations and functions are not stable or predictable anymore and this allows the labour force to exist in a complex and uncertain market. Consequently, the need for employees to develop their own capacity to innovate, adapt to change, and manage this emerging instability is germane. There are several market dynamics that impact labour market, such as demographic development, the competitiveness of the nations’ economy, globalization and last but not the least is technological change or digitalization. Research showed that the technological revolution, however, is of great significance. The technological transformation is a prevailing factor out of the four listed (Messina. Artificial Intelligence and digital transformation have revolutionized the strategies that are deployed by both public and private organizations to relate with their customers, and specifically how companies run their business, how they conceive their business approach and how they consolidate their operations. It is about integrating digital technologies, such as social, mobile, analytics and cloud, in the service of transforming how businesses work. Although it is important to state that the incorporation of digital technology into business processes has become very imperative for the survival and competitive advantage of contemporary organizations, Human Capital Management (HCM) focuses on the performance of the organization emphasizing its role as a solution to business problems in the post-automation economy. Therefore, designing job roles in the post-automation economy is a strategic asset to businesses contributing to the competitive advantage of organizations. Thus, the entirety of this paper is centered on a more varied, more people-oriented with the responsibility of designing diverse, challenging jobs in the post-automation economy to keep the human element more active and engaged in their work without redundancy. The paper strongly maintained that Human Capital Management is to assume more active roles in handling the post-automation, digitalization and the age of AI era in ensuring that the human element is skilled and knowledgeable to meet the future needs of the organizations

items.title: Zero-shot mineral segmentation in reflected-light microscopy using the segment anything model
items.abstract: Automated mineral segmentation underpins quantitative mineralogy and stereological characterization, but supervised deep-learning methods require annotated data and may generalize poorly across mineralogical domains. This study evaluated the Segment Anything Model (SAM), a general-purpose foundation model, for reflected-light microscopy (RLM) mineral-image analysis in a purely zero-shot setting, without task-specific training, fine-tuning, or domain adaptation. Two complementary case studies were conducted. First, three SAM encoder variants (ViT-B, ViT-L, and ViT-H) were evaluated on publicly available iron-ore (FeM) and copper-ore (Cu) RLM datasets using SEM-derived reference masks. SAM achieved mean F1-scores of 0.77–0.88, with ViT-L and ViT-H reaching 93–94% of the previously reported supervised DeepLabv3+ F1-score benchmark for FeM and approximately 93% for Cu. Second, SAM was applied to polarized RLM image stacks of dolomite to assess its influence on downstream stereological characterization. No significant differences from the gradient-based method were detected for any RGB configuration or PCA ViT-B in major or minor intercept length or bireflectance. The largest deviations occurred for PCA-preprocessed ViT-H, with median major and minor intercept lengths approximately 21% and 17% higher, respectively, and bireflectance approximately 16% lower. No significant method-dependent difference was detected in principal anisotropy orientation. These results show that zero-shot SAM can support mineral-image segmentation and downstream stereological characterization without annotated training data, while highlighting the influence of preprocessing and encoder choice on the derived grain representation

items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into social practice has been accompanied by the emergence of new forms of unlawful conduct, requiring a reconsideration of traditional institutions of criminal law. The most challenging cases for criminal-law qualification arise where an AI system operates with partial or full autonomy, independently determining the means of achieving a goal set by a human. In such situations, establishing a causal link between the user’s conduct and the resulting socially dangerous consequences does not, in itself, constitute a sufficient basis for criminal liability, thereby raising the issue of the limits of subjective attribution. Based on the normative framework of the 2021 Criminal Code of the Republic of Armenia governing guilt, mistake as to factual circumstances, harm caused without guilt, and justified risk, the article argues that AI cannot be recognized as an independent subject of criminal liability. To determine the limits of criminal-law attribution, the author distinguishes three models of criminally relevant use of AI: the instrumental model (AI as a means of implementing criminal intent), the risk-based model (the use of AI in circumstances where the possibility of a socially dangerous consequence is foreseen or ought to be foreseen), and the autonomous-result model (the occurrence of a result that was not encompassed by the person’s intent and whose possibility the person was neither required nor able to foresee). The principle of controlled autonomy formulated in the article makes it possible to determine the boundary between culpable harm caused by a human and a result of the autonomous operation of an intelligent system that cannot be attributed to that person.

items.abstract: This article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations for using marketing analytics as a tool for strategic decision-making in advertising management in the context of sustainable development. The relevance of this study stems from the digital transformation of marketing activities, the growth in data volumes, the increasing complexity of consumer behavior models, and the need to shift from evaluating advertising activities primarily based on economic criteria to a comprehensive consideration of the economic, social, and environmental outcomes of advertising strategies. The role of marketing analytics as a component of the information and analytical support for strategic advertising management is substantiated; its functional purpose lies in transforming marketing data into relevant information for justifying, selecting, and adjusting strategic decisions. The functional purpose of descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics in the process of developing advertising strategies is revealed. The paper identifies opportunities for applying artificial intelligence, machine learning, and predictive modeling technologies to segment target audiences, personalize advertising messages, forecast consumer behavior, and optimize advertising investments. The paper justifies the need to integrate the principles of sustainable development into the system for evaluating the effectiveness of advertising strategies. It proposes a system of indicators structured around economic, social, and environmental components, which makes it possible to take into account – alongside the commercial effectiveness of advertising investments – brand trust, responsibility and transparency of advertising communications, the impact on the formation of sustainable consumption patterns, the environmental impact of advertising activities, and the risks of greenwashing. For a comprehensive assessment, an integral index of sustainable advertising strategy performance (ISRAS) is proposed, which involves aggregating normalized indicators of economic, social, and environmental performance and can be used for a multi-criteria comparison of alternative advertising strategies. To illustrate the ISRAS application algorithm, a demonstration calculation was performed using two hypothetical scenarios of IKEA’s advertising strategy and model normalized values. Scientific and practical recommendations have been formulated for improving the strategic decision-making process in advertising management based on an integrated analytical and strategic approach that encompasses analytical diagnosis, the formulation of strategic alternatives, their multi-criteria evaluation, the selection and implementation of an advertising strategy, monitoring, and strategic adjustments. The feasibility of transitioning from a piecemeal assessment of advertising campaign effectiveness to a comprehensive evaluation of the sustained effectiveness of advertising strategies has been substantiated. The potential for integrating marketing analytics and the principles of sustainable development has been identified to enhance the soundness of strategic advertising decisions, optimize marketing resources, strengthen consumer trust, minimize reputational and environmental risks, and create long-term value for the enterprise, consumers, and society.

items.title: “Word‐By‐Word” or “Line‐By‐Line” Presentation? How Response Generation Dynamics in Generative AI Influence User Acceptance
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Generative AI systems are increasingly integrated into various user support and decision‐making contexts. While extensive research has explored user acceptance of generative AI across domains, less is known about how its inherent presentation features influence such acceptance. This study investigates how the presentation format of generative AI responses—high‐dynamism formats (word‐by‐word) versus low‐dynamism formats (line‐by‐line)—affects users' willingness to accept its output. Three experiments, across various contexts, including daily question‐answering, online shopping, and crowdfunding platforms, tested how the dynamic presentation of generative AI responses influences users' willingness to accept its output. The results demonstrate that users exhibit greater receptivity when generative AI responses are presented in high‐dynamism formats. This effect occurs because dynamic presentation enhances users' feelings of immersion. Furthermore, we find that users' situational need for understanding moderates this immersion‐based mechanism. Specifically, the positive indirect effect of dynamic presentation on willingness to accept the output through feelings of immersion is attenuated in high need‐for‐understanding contexts, where users tend to prioritize content quality, accuracy, and diagnosticity. In contrast, this indirect effect is amplified in low need‐for‐understanding contexts, where users are more receptive to the experiential and interactional qualities of dynamic presentation. This research contributes to the literature on the effectiveness of dynamic presentation and provides novel insights into the factors influencing user acceptance of generative AI outputs. Our findings highlight the importance of tailoring output presentation methods based on individual user characteristics and task‐specific cognitive demands.

items.title: 346 Dead - and Boeing Is Still Asking Pilots to Work Around the Software
items.abstract: The Boeing 737 MAX disasters killed 346 people and exposed profound failures involving aircraft design, automation, human-factors assumptions, corporate safety culture, and federal regulatory oversight. This article examines those failures against the emergence of a new flight-management-system software defect capable of disengaging vertical navigation (VNAV) during certain missed-approach sequences on affected 737 MAX aircraft. Rather than equating the VNAV issue with the catastrophic MCAS failures, the analysis considers a more fundamental question: whether Boeing and the Federal Aviation Administration have adequately incorporated the lessons of the MAX accidents when known automation deficiencies can still be mitigated through increased pilot workload while permanent engineering corrections remain pending. The investigation further examines Boeing’s criminal-accountability history, including the federal fraud charge, deferred prosecution agreement, subsequent determination that Boeing breached that agreement, proposed guilty plea, and eventual non-prosecution agreement. Particular attention is given to Boeing’s extensive political presence, campaign and inaugural contributions, federal lobbying, regulatory relationships, and its selection for major next-generation U.S. fighter programs. No evidence examined establishes a quid pro quo between Boeing’s political activities, prosecutorial outcomes, or defense contracts; however, the record reveals substantial structural interdependence between Boeing and the federal institutions responsible for regulating, prosecuting, and purchasing from the company. The article argues that after 346 deaths, reliance upon pilots to compensate procedurally for correctable automation deficiencies deserves exceptional scrutiny and that Boeing’s strategic importance should not insulate the corporation or its decision-makers from meaningful regulatory and criminal accountability.

items.abstract: 3D concrete printing (3DCP) has revolutionized the construction industry, allowing for the produc-tion of complex geometries with greater efficiency and sustainability. This is despite ongoing challenges with structural reliability and long-term performance, which are due to the material's anisotropic properties and layer interfaces.This study performed a bibliometric analysis of the literature on the structural analysis of 3DCP, using VOSviewer to identify research trends and gaps. The methodology included a keyword search in the Scopus database, which resulted in 108 selected articles after a rigorous screening process. The results in-dicate a significant increase in 3DCP research since 2018, with a projected peak of 40 articles published in 2025. A co-occurrence analysis of keywords revealed a concentration on "concretes," "concrete printings," and "finite element method," highlighting research into material failure and behavior. The 108 works, au-thored by 374 individuals, were distributed across 8 clusters, with 23 papers showing co-authorship. Maximil-iano Cremonesi, Liberato Ferrara, and Giacomo Rizzieri had the strongest collaborations between 2024 and 2025. China and the United States lead in publications, with 37 and 12 articles, respectively, and China also leads in collaborations with 14. The Journal of Building Engineering was the most relevant journal, with 11 publications. Despite these advancements, the study points to significant gaps, such as the need for more so-phisticated numerical models to simulate interlayer and multi-scale interactions. The integration of structural reinforcements and a better understanding of the long-term durability of 3DCP are also critical challenges. Furthermore, there is a major opportunity for research in multifunctional materials and the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning to optimize design and predict performance, thereby boosting sus-tainability in 3DCP.

items.title: A Critical African Examination of Nick Bostrom's Conception of the Problem of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has generated profound philosophical questions concerning intelligence, agency, autonomy, responsibility, human values, technological power, and the future of humanity. Among contemporary philosophers, Nick Bostrom has provided one of the most systematic philosophical analyses of the long-term risks associated with advanced artificial intelligence. His conception of the problem is principally concerned with the possibility that artificial general intelligence may develop into superintelligence whose cognitive and strategic capacities surpass those of human beings. The central difficulty, according to Bostrom, is not merely whether machines can think, but whether humanity can retain meaningful control over machines that may eventually become more intelligent and strategically capable than their creators. This article critically examined Bostrom's conception of the problem of artificial intelligence, focusing on his notions of superintelligence, existential risk, the orthogonality thesis, instrumental convergence, and the control problem. It argued that Bostrom's analysis provides an important conceptual foundation for contemporary debates on artificial intelligence safety and alignment but requires philosophical supplementation when considered from an African perspective. In particular, the individualistic assumptions that can underlie some formulations of artificial intelligence ethics require enrichment through African conceptions of communal responsibility, relational personhood, human dignity, and social embeddedness. The article concluded that Bostrom's conception of artificial intelligence is philosophically valuable as a theory of technological control and existential risk, but its relevance to Africa is strengthened when integrated with relational and communitarian conceptions of personhood and responsibility. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Nick Bostrom, superintelligence, existential risk, alignment, control problem, African philosophy.

items.title: A generative AI decision-making tool for interactive greenspace design using a pollinator habitat indicator
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in landscape architecture to accelerate design development and enhance stakeholder engagement. This study presents a new landscape concept design tool to support collaborative greenspace problem-solving by integrating rapid scenario generation with a Pollinator Habitat Indicator (PHI). We define this as the PHI-AI Landscape Design Tool. The model combines text-to-image generative workflows with a simplified pollinator-oriented reference that compares AI-generated scenarios based on broad landscape cover composition. The PHI-AI Landscape Design Tool generated varied concept layouts with planting and pathway configurations responsive to descriptive prompts and user-defined parameters. It generates layout variations that reflect visually coherent planting configurations, and circulation connections to existing infrastructure for user functionality. This enables the rapid production of multiple design alternatives that remain legible, adaptable, and flexible to human-controlled editing prompts for stakeholder engagement. This study offers a framework for integrating a simplified ecological reference into the planning phase of landscape design.

items.title: A human-centred artificial intelligence and learning analytics framework for equitable personalised higher education enrolment
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are increasingly deployed within higher education to support admissions decision-making, student success initiatives, and personalised learning. However, most AI-enabled admissions systems remain narrowly focused on efficiency, prediction, and institutional optimisation, with limited attention to learner agency, educational equity, transparency, and human-centred support. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that repositions admissions as the beginning of a personalised learning journey rather than merely a selection or gatekeeping process. The study adopts a conceptual and integrative literature review approach, synthesising scholarship from human-centred artificial intelligence, learning analytics, personalised learning, educational equity, explainable AI, generative AI, responsible AI governance, learner agency theory, and value-sensitive design. To strengthen transparency during revision, the integrative synthesis was supplemented by a targeted ERIC search and bibliographic verification using publisher and authoritative policy repositories. Drawing upon these interdisciplinary perspectives, the paper develops the Human-Centred Personalised Admissions Framework (HCPAF), a governance-oriented model for ethical and transparent AI adoption in higher education admissions and enrolment management. The framework comprises five interconnected dimensions: learner profiling and contextual understanding; explainable AI decision support; equity and inclusion auditing; human oversight and shared decision-making; and personalised transition and success support. Together, these dimensions provide a governance architecture for evaluating how admissions might be connected to personalised educational pathways while making explicit the trade-offs among equity, privacy, explainability, accuracy, human oversight, and learner agency. The framework identifies governance mechanisms required to address algorithmic bias, transparency, privacy, accountability, and learner autonomy. A five-stage Human-Centred AI Ecosystem extending governance across the full student lifecycle — from admissions through to graduate development — provides a further organising contribution. The study advances existing literature by integrating admissions analytics, learning analytics, personalised learning, learner agency, and responsible AI governance within a unified framework. Unlike conventional admissions models that prioritise institutional efficiency, HCPAF positions admissions as the foundation of a personalised learning ecosystem and conceptualises trust as a relational, calibrated, and empirically contingent construct connecting transparency, fairness, learner agency, and AI adoption. The framework contributes to emerging debates concerning ethical and human-centred AI in education and identifies normative alignments with Sustainable Development Goals 4, 10, and 16, while emphasising that any contribution to those goals requires empirical validation. Introduces the Human-Centred Personalised Admissions Framework (HCPAF) for equitable and personalised higher education enrolment. Repositions admissions as the beginning of a personalised learning journey rather than a terminal selection mechanism. Integrates human-centred AI, learning analytics, educational equity, explainable AI, learner agency, and responsible governance. Introduces trust as a central mediating construct linking transparency, fairness, and AI adoption in education. Provides a governance roadmap for ethical, transparent, and accountable AI adoption across the student lifecycle. Identifies normative alignments with Sustainable Development Goals 4 (Quality Education), 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions), subject to empirical validation. Establishes a multi-dimensional research agenda for human-centred AI in higher education.

items.title: A reproducible audit of a cumulative zone of theoretical visibility with open data: Scout Moor II and Calderdale Energy Park
items.abstract: Working paper, data and code. Scout Moor II (12 turbines up to 180 m to blade tip, Rossendale and Rochdale, applications 2025/0267 and 25/00680/FUL) and Calderdale Energy Park (34 turbines in its April 2026 preliminary environmental information report) are proposed on the South Pennines with their nearest turbines 15.7 km apart. The paper builds a cumulative zone of theoretical visibility for the two schemes entirely from open data (OS Terrain 50 at 50 m, eye 2 m, refraction coefficient 0.075, 45 km from each turbine, a single blade tip counts) and checks it against the applicants' own figures and software. On bare earth, 698.9 km² of land sees at least one turbine of each scheme; the applicant's own QGIS plugin, given the same inputs, gives 685.4 km², and one sight line per cell gives 664.4 km². Where both models compute, the applicant's own combined map (Further Environmental Information Figure 11.16) agrees with the model (intersection over union 0.88). The paper then tests what screening does. On the Environment Agency's first-return LIDAR surface, the combined view is lost at 49 of the 51 highest-scoring settlement points at the point itself, and kept at 17 on a small grid of observers around the point (12 counting only observers within 100 m). On the applicant's own screening rule, rebuilt from the notes on its Figures 11.7 and 11.8 with the observer on the ground, 174.9 km² of the 206.7 km² of its "both may be visible" class within 20 km keeps the view, and 35 of the 62 settlement points in that class. What went against the author is reported in the main text: the cell rule, the ground-level rule, a re-sited viewpoint, the screening results, the roof-observer error found by a hostile read, the errors of the first-round objection and their correction, and four errors of wording in the round-two documents, one of them corrected on the site. The deposit contains the paper (Markdown), the model and its tests, every model output, the representation and articles as sent or published, the audit, review and method records, and a source manifest citing every applicant document by URL and SHA-256 rather than copying it. reproduce.py checks the inputs, can rebuild every grid from the open data in three tiers, and recomputes 408 figures, some a second way; tools/check_paper.py checks every model figure quoted in the paper, the representation, its appendices and the article against that output. Run "uv run python reproduce.py", then "uv run python tools/check_paper.py". The author objected to the Scout Moor II applications in a personal capacity and as county councillor for Padiham and Burnley West, Lancashire County Council, and is the council's Cabinet Member for Adult Social Care; see the Declaration of Interests. The applications are live; the paper describes a method and its checks and takes no position on the decision. The research and checks were carried out by AI agents (Anthropic's Claude) working for the author; no human peer review has taken place. Version 1.0. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23138011. items.title: A review of open-vocabulary semantic mapping and navigation with foundation models for mobile robots
items.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots that coexist with humans must construct not only geometric maps but also semantic maps that can be accessed through natural language. Conventional semantic mapping has mainly focused on assigning labels from predefined closed vocabularies to metric maps, limiting its ability to handle novel objects, open-ended linguistic expressions, and flexible human-robot interaction. Recent advances in large-scale foundation models, particularly LLMs and VLMs, have accelerated research on open-vocabulary semantic mapping. In parallel, generative 3D representations such as neural radiance fields and 3D Gaussian splatting have enabled dense, continuous spatial representations associated with language-derived features. Together, these developments allow robots to acquire spatial semantic representations that connect perception, language, and action. This paper reviews this rapidly evolving field through a four-part taxonomy: (i) fusion of semantic features into 3D metric maps; (ii) object-centric open-vocabulary representations; (iii) hierarchical scene graph representations; and (iv) continuous generative 3D language fields. We also revisit the history of open-vocabulary semantic mapping and provide an overview of foundation model-based navigation using language-accessible maps, ranging from object-goal navigation to LLM-based hierarchical task planning. Finally, we introduce evaluation datasets, simulators, robot platforms, and evaluation metrics, and summarize seven open challenges.

items.title: A Survey of Computer Vision Applications in Industrial Environments
items.abstract: In recent years, Computer Vision (CV) has evolved rapidly, enabling enhanced automation, safety, inspection, and logistics across manufacturing, construction, and robotics. This systematic review surveys current computer vision applications in industrial environments, spanning factory defect inspection, construction-site safety, warehouse inventory tracking, and industrial robotics. From more than 8,700 initially identified studies, we selected 146 key papers representing cross-domain CV applications. The survey is organized into four thematic areas: visual inspection and defect detection, worker safety and monitoring, inventory and logistics tracking, and robotics and automation. For each area, we compare state-of-the-art approaches, datasets, and deployment settings while highlighting the factors that influence their performance under different operating conditions. For example, YOLO-based detectors dominate real-time edge deployment because of their high throughput, whereas transformer-based models often struggle to scale in resource-constrained environments despite their superior feature extraction capabilities. We also identify critical research gaps. Although manufacturing and construction benefit from numerous public datasets for quality inspection and safety monitoring, warehousing and robotics continue to lack large-scale, real-world benchmark datasets. Finally, we discuss emerging research directions, including domain adaptation, edge AI, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), to support the development of more robust, scalable, and balanced computer vision solutions for industrial applications.

items.title: ACAAI - Accountability by Design for Agentic AI: A Lifecycle Framework for Engineering Accountability in Autonomous AI Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly evolving from systems that generate recommendations and content towards autonomous agents capable of planning, reasoning, interacting with external systems, using tools and executing actions with limited human intervention. As AI systems become more agentic, accountability can no longer be understood solely as a legal obligation or post-incident governance exercise. It must also become an operational property embedded into the design, deployment and operation of autonomous AI systems. ACAAI (Accountability by Design for Agentic AI) approaches accountability as a systems engineering property that emerges from the coordinated implementation of organizational and technical controls rather than from any single governance mechanism. Building upon principles from AI governance, cybersecurity, safety engineering, resilience engineering and AI assurance, the framework translates existing governance principles into more than 100 organizational and technical controls spanning the lifecycle of agentic AI systems. ACAAI is structured around six complementary control domains: (1) Organizational Governance, (2) Human Oversight, Consent and Decision Authority, (3) Identity, Authority and Data Governance, (4) Observability, Explainability and Evidence, (5) Runtime Safety and Assurance, and (6) Incident Response and Recovery. Rather than proposing a new regulatory model or prescriptive implementation methodology, ACAAI provides a structured engineering foundation for designing, deploying, operating and retiring accountable autonomous AI systems. The framework also dentifies research and implementation challenges that remain as agentic AI systems become increasingly autonomous, interconnected and collaborative.

items.title: Agent Execution Control Planes: When 'Sandbox', 'Gateway', and 'Policy' Ship as Unauthenticated Code Execution
items.abstract: An empirical, runtime-verified study of the 'execution control plane' layer of the AI-agent ecosystem: services named agent-exec-gateway, agent-sandbox, code-sandbox, or policy engine that are supposed to constrain agent execution by policy, approval, and isolation. Scanning ~500 freshly-published MCP/A2A/agent repositories across five attack-surface dimensions (supply-chain poisoning, permission-escaping, credential storage, prompt-injection defense, protocol implementation), we confirm and responsibly disclose 4 exploitable vulnerabilities whose shared root cause is 'control-plane trust inversion': the component named for restriction ships as an unauthenticated, direct code-execution endpoint (CWE-306), enabling policy bypass and arbitrary command/Python execution with output read-back. A control group of seven hardened implementations (fail-closed boot, constant-time HMAC compare, single-use approval, gvisor/VM isolation) shows the ecosystem is two-sided: established agent infrastructure is hardened while freshly-published 0-star 'control-plane' repositories repeatedly invert the trust model. We provide detection signatures, honest deployment-boundary analysis (loopback vs 0.0.0.0 Docker), and hardening guidance.

items.title: AGI: How It Could Change Humanity's Role in Society
items.abstract: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) refers to a kind of artificial intelligence that is able to learn, reason, and perform a wide range of intellectual tasks at the same or better levels as humans do. This paper explores the implications that AGI might have on humanity if it was to become a reality, especially its effects on work, society, and human dependency on intelligent machines. However, the scope of the discussion does not focus on whether AGI would replace human labor, but rather on whether humans would be less central to the organization of society.

items.title: AI and the "end of the world"
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence advances at an unprecedented pace, the conversation surrounding its potential to destroy humanity often revolves around science fiction scenarios, rogue machines, and autonomous weapons. But what if the greatest threat isn't AI turning against us, but a world that becomes so dependent on it that we can no longer function without it? In AI and the "End of the World," Simon Abayomi Olawuyi explores a hypothetical future where AI permeates every aspect of human existence, from critical infrastructure and personal identity to employment, information, and the very concept of truth. Through a speculative look at the road from the 2022 AI boom to 2035, the piece examines a different kind of existential risk: a society so deeply intertwined with artificial intelligence that disconnecting from it could become more dangerous than keeping it running.

items.title: AI Literacy and Future Skills Readiness Among Employees: A Human Resource Management Perspective
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday work has made employees' ability to understand, evaluate and collaborate with AI systems a strategic human resource. This paper asks how employees' AI literacy relates to their readiness for the future skills that employers increasingly demand, and how AI self-efficacy and organisational training support shape that relationship. The study proceeds in two phases. Study 1 synthesises published workforce evidence from the World Economic Forum (2025), Microsoft and LinkedIn (2024), the OECD (2024) and the Federal Reserve (2024, 2025), documenting a structural 'demand-readiness gap' in which demand for AI-fluent employees outpaces structured training provision. analyses an illustrative, calibrated employee dataset (N = 384) using measurement validation, hierarchical regression, bootstrapped mediation and moderation analysis. AI literacy was positively associated with future skills readiness (beta = 0.70, p < .001), and AI self-efficacy partially mediated this association (indirect effect = 0.13, 95% bootstrap CI [0.08, 0.18]). Organisational training support strengthened the literacy-readiness association (interaction beta = 0.18, p < .001), such that the relationship was significant under high support but weaker under low support. Human-AI collaboration and critical evaluation emerged as the strongest literacy dimensions, and readiness differed significantly across job functions. The study positions AI literacy as organisationally contingent human capital and proposes a training-architecture framework for HRM. Findings are directional and should be read in light of the simulated nature of the dataset.

items.title: AI Translation between Interpretation and Hallucination – Evidence for the Evaluative Competence of Vietnamese Students
items.abstract: Generative AI complicates translation evaluation because fluent outputs may introduce unsupported meaning, while non-literal renderings may represent legitimate interpretation. This study examined Vietnamese EFL students’ evaluation of AI-generated translations and its associations with digital competence, translation competence, and critical-evaluation confidence. A cross-sectional study involved 213 final-year English majors who completed a 25-item performance task and self-report scales. Students were considerably more accurate in recognising problematic outputs than in diagnosing their type (68.0% vs. 38.4%). Critical-evaluation confidence showed the strongest association with performance (r=.85), although its conceptual overlap with the performance task warrants caution. In the full regression model, translation competence (β=.31) and digital competence (β=.16) contributed significantly alongside critical-evaluation confidence (β=.64), whereas AI-use frequency did not. When the overlapping critical-evaluation measure was removed, the model still explained 55% of performance variance, with translation competence showing the strongest association (β=.61). The findings indicate that evaluating AI-generated translation depends less on frequency of AI use than on students’ translation knowledge and evaluative judgement, particularly their ability to distinguish unsupported generation from defensible interpretation. Rather than simply as a translation tool Generative AI should thus be used as an object of critical inquiry. Alternative AI renderings may expose students to interpretations they had not considered, including potentially productive expansions of source meaning. This approach preserves the interpretive character of translation while making students accountable for the decisions they ultimately accept.

items.title: AI vs. human authorship in paintings: Differential impacts on consumers' perceived value Guangdong Provincial Graduate Education Innovation Program Project: Research on the Evaluation Index System for Practical Innovation Ability of Professional Degree Graduate Students (2024JGXM-076)
items.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) art generators has introduced algorithmically created paintings into mainstream consumer markets, yet consumers consistently assign lower value to AI-generated works than to human-created equivalents. This paper proposes perceived creative authenticity---consumers' subjective perception that an artwork reflects a genuine creative process characterized by human-centered values of originality, craftsmanship, and uniqueness---as a theoretically distinct mechanism explaining this value differential. Conceptually differentiated from perceived creativity, which concerns the novelty of the artistic output, perceived creative authenticity addresses the genuineness of the creator-work relationship. Drawing on authenticity theory and Psychological Ownership Theory, we develop a moderated mediation framework hypothesizing that (H1) human authorship elicits higher perceived value than AI authorship, (H2) perceived creative authenticity mediates this effect, while the indirect effects through perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs are not significant, establishing perceived creative authenticity as the primary explanatory mechanism within the tested model, and (H3) non-fungible token (NFT) authentication attenuates the mediated pathway by providing verifiable creative provenance. Across five studies, results support this framework: Study 1 conceptually replicates the human-AI value gap among Chinese consumers; Studies 2a—2c demonstrate the mediating role of perceived creative authenticity: Study 2a establishes the basic mediation pathway; Study 2b shows through parallel mediation that perceived creative authenticity uniquely mediates the effect while perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs do not exhibit significant indirect effects; and Study 2c provides causal evidence through a moderation-of-process design; and Study 3 shows that NFT authentication narrows the authenticity gap between human and AI art. items.title: AI-Augmented Succession Planning in Volunteer Organizations
items.abstract: Volunteer organizations play a critical role in civil society, yet many face increasing difficulty finding, developing, and replacing volunteer leaders. Demographic change, evolving patterns of civic participation, competing demands on volunteers’ time, and volunteer fatigue create significant challenges for leadership continuity. Although succession planning has been extensively studied in corporate and professional contexts, less attention has been given to volunteer organizations, where authority, engagement, and leadership development operate differently.This article examines succession challenges in volunteer organizations and argues that succession planning should be understood as an ongoing responsibility of governance and stewardship rather than a response to leadership vacancies. Drawing on literature concerning succession planning, nonprofit leadership, volunteer management, social capital, and civic engagement, the article proposes an actionable six-step model emphasizing leadership commitment, role clarity, succession-risk assessment, identification and development of potential successors, and redesign of leadership roles to strengthen continuity and leadership pipelines. A hypothetical community arts organization illustrates the model’s practical application.The article further examines how artificial intelligence can augment succession planning in resource-constrained volunteer organizations through knowledge capture, role clarification, leadership development, and continuity planning. AI is conceptualized as a capacity-building tool rather than a substitute for human judgment. Volunteer leaders remain responsible for organizational context, confidentiality, fairness, governance, and succession decisions. The resulting approach positions AI-augmented succession planning as a human-centered strategy for strengthening leadership continuity, institutional knowledge, and organizational resilience.

items.title: AI-Driven Encryption and Resource Optimization in Cloud Security Frameworks
items.abstract: Abstract Cloud-based systems demand secure yet efficient file access mechanisms. Traditional encryption frameworks often introduce latency and resource overhead, limiting scalability. Building on Astillero's (2026) AI-driven logic gate synthesis, this paper explores how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can optimize encrypted file access. By applying Reinforcement Learning (RL), Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), and Large Circuit Models (LCMs), AI enables adaptive encryption, predictive access control, and efficient resource allocation. This study also integrates recent research on AI-based workload management and reinforcement learning for secure access control, highlighting how intelligent systems can balance security, scalability, and performance.

items.title: AI-Driven People Analytics and Employee Retention: Assessing The Role of Data-Driven HR Decision-Making
items.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance employee retention amidst significant turnover issues in modern organizations. It conducts a systematic review of 58 sources, including peer-reviewed articles and practitioner reports, predominantly from 2015 to 2026, and proposes an integrative conceptual framework. The findings indicate a discrepancy between improved predictive accuracy for voluntary turnover and inconsistent retention gains, particularly in organizations with advanced analytics capabilities. Resistance from employees often stems from concerns about fairness, transparency, and surveillance. The study introduces a dual-pathway model: the enabling pathway, where analytics lead to interventions that enhance job embeddedness and retention, and the evaluative pathway, where perceptions of justice and privacy can undermine these benefits. The paper advances nine propositions detailing these relationships and uniquely integrates four existing research areas—HR analytics, algorithmic management, organizational justice, and turnover theory—reconceptualizing retention analytics as a matter of decision quality and legitimacy rather than mere predictive accuracy. It lays out a research agenda for future empirical inquiries and offers practical recommendations for ethical AI deployment in HR decision-making.

items.title: AI, decision and healthy work
items.abstract: This paper explores the architectural novelty of artificial intelligence (AI) and its implications for occupational health as both a field of practice and a domain of organisational design. Unlike previous general-purpose technologies such as databases, AI operates through stochastic modelling of normative patterns, generating predictions rather than retrieving stored information. This fundamental difference makes AI simultaneously powerful and limited: it can codify norms but struggles with specificity, nuance, and contextual variation central to occupational health decision-making. Drawing on management science, systems theory, and social theory, the paper contrasts two key organisational questions: how to use AI within existing structures, and how to reorganise occupational health given that AI exists. It argues that the latter question, aligned with Stafford Beer’s systems thinking, is essential for responsible and effective adoption. AI’s greatest potential lies not in automation, but in enhancing organisational perception—of human relations, meaning in research, social and spatial dynamics—functioning as a new kind of scientific instrument that amplifies reflexivity and end-to-end “flow.” The paper concludes that sustainable integration of AI in occupational health demands socio-technical design, responsible innovation frameworks, and a focus on organisational learning to maintain healthy, adaptive workplaces in an era of technological transformation.

items.title: An integrated scientometric and BERTopic-based analysis on examining the role of artificial intelligence in achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
items.abstract: This study investigates the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through a comprehensive scientometric analysis. It explores the evolution of scholarly research, identifies leading contributors, maps thematic trends, examines how AI technologies contribute to advancing sustainability across multiple domains, and identifies latent semantic themes. A total of 3262 unique scholarly records published between 1989 and 2025, after deduplication and screening, were finalized from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. The dataset was analysed using Biblioshiny (R-based Bibliometrix) and VOSviewer to examine publication trends, citation impact, collaborative networks, thematic evolution, and conceptual structures. Indicators such as Relative Growth Rate (RGR), Doubling Time (DT), h-index, g-index, and Lotka’s Law were applied to evaluate research productivity and scholarly influence. In addition, BERTopic-based abstract-level topic modelling was applied to identify latent semantic themes, SDG-linked thematic domains, temporal evolution and potential research gaps. Results reveal a significant growth in AI-SDG research, particularly after 2015, with an accelerated increase post-2020. India, USA, and China emerged as the most productive contributors, while countries like USA, India, United Kingdom and Australia lead in research impact and citation quality. Thematic evolution analysis reveals a transition from foundational themes such as AI, machine learning, climate change, and decision support systems toward more integrated and sustainability-oriented research themes, including sustainable development and SDGs. Thematic linkages further demonstrate the persistent foundational role of AI and machine learning, alongside the growing centrality of climate change and sustainable development, reflecting the increasing convergence of AI research with global sustainability priorities. BERTopic analysis further revealed eleven interpretable abstract-level thematic domains after excluding one heterogeneous outlier category. The dominant themes included digital transformation and green innovation, AI-enabled education, digital health, smart agriculture, renewable energy systems, clean water and sanitation, remote sensing, NLP-based decision support, sustainable construction, tourism, and sustainable chemistry/pharmaceutical applications. This study maps the AI–SDG research landscape by integrating bibliometric indicators with thematic evolution, conceptual analysis, and abstract-level semantic topic modelling. The findings provide insights into the development and thematic orientation of AI-related research in the context of sustainable development. The use of BERTopic complements conventional bibliometric approaches by examining semantic patterns within publication abstracts alongside keyword and citation-based analyses.

items.title: Analytics and AI in Management
items.abstract: The modern business world is changing rapidly with the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and predictive analytics. Earlier, businesses depended mainly on past data to understand what had already happened. Today, AI and analytics help organizations predict future situations and make better decisions based on available data. This change has given rise to the idea of “augmented intelligence”, in which AI works together with people to support their decisions instead of replacing them. This paper studies how the use of AI and predictive analytics is affecting businesses and the way managers make decisions. It focuses on the use of AI in daily work, the automation of routine tasks, access to analytical tools and the changing role of human judgment in decision-making. A survey of 35 management professionals (N = 35) was conducted to understand their practical experience of AI and analytics in the workplace. The results show that AI is already being used in many professional roles: about 88.6% of respondents said that their work involves both AI and analytics, and 82.9% said that AI has significantly reduced their workload.

items.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence Feedback in College English Writing Assessment
items.abstract: In the fast-changing digital education and the rapid development of artificial intelligence, AI-generated feedback has been widely used in college English writing assessment as a valuable teaching support. The traditional manual marking is typically characterized by a heavy workload, slow feedback, and subjective judgment, making it difficult to meet students’ individual needs for writing improvement. AI feedback can detect surface-level language errors and improve the efficiency of assessment because it can provide immediate feedback, follow standard correction procedures, and offer detailed diagnostic guidance, thereby helping students to revise their writing autonomously. In this study, the analysis of student essays titled “The Impact of Influencer Culture on Youth Consumption Patterns” will be done to evaluate the utility of feedback provided by artificial intelligence. Additionally, rule-based AI correction and a more detailed review by teachers considering the practical value and importance of the learning process will be applied. It is proved that AI is quite efficient when dealing with language mistakes, yet it is insufficient in the logical development of an essay, in-depth interpretation, and critical thinking that are still the responsibility of teachers. From the author’s teaching experience, a new model that combines the efforts of AI and teachers can be proposed, according to which AI makes surface-level corrections and teachers concentrate on developing the higher-order skills of students.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and occupational medicine
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping occupational medicine through applications in automation, smart monitoring, extended reality training, algorithmic management, and digital work arrangements. The EASOM Summer School 2025 examined how AI technologies enhance occupational health systems by enabling real-time risk identification, predictive surveillance, and targeted interventions to prevent work-related accidents and diseases. Practical applications include smart personal protective equipment, wearable sensors, augmented reality training systems, and predictive diagnostics exemplified by noise-related hearing loss risk assessment. However, significant challenges accompany these opportunities: data quality concerns, new technological hazards, psychosocial risks including surveillance-related stress and work intensification, algorithmic bias, and accountability gaps. Implementation requires comprehensive governance frameworks emphasizing early worker involvement, privacy-by-design approaches, phased pilot programs, and human-centered practices that complement rather than replace traditional occupational safety measures. Professional responsibility and education demand new competencies in digital literacy, algorithmic critical thinking, and applied ethics while maintaining essential clinical judgment and empathy. AI offers unprecedented potential for protecting workers' health and safety when responsibly implemented within transparent frameworks, but poor management risks deepening inequalities and eroding established protections. Successful integration depends on multidisciplinary research, international cooperation, stakeholder engagement, and a commitment to human-centered occupational medicine that prioritizes worker dignity and wellbeing.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Anxiety and Employee Performance: A Systematic Literature Review of Job Insecurity, Threat–Challenge Appraisal, Coping, Career Resilience, and Organisational Buffers
items.abstract: This systematic literature review examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety and employee performance, with particular attention to job insecurity, threat–challenge appraisal, coping, career resilience, job crafting, leadership, training, organisational support, and human–AI collaboration. The review synthesises publicly accessible scholarly evidence and a supplied research corpus using multiple conceptual search strategies and backward and forward citation searching. The evidence is organised around two complementary pathways. The first is a threat pathway, in which AI-related concerns about job replacement, skill obsolescence, loss of autonomy, and employment continuity may contribute to anxiety, job insecurity, emotional exhaustion, withdrawal, and weaker performance-related outcomes. The second is an opportunity pathway, in which AI is appraised as a manageable challenge and can support learning, job crafting, adaptation, engagement, and performance when appropriate personal and organisational resources are available. The review integrates Cognitive Appraisal Theory, Conservation of Resources Theory, and Job Demands–Resources theory to explain why employee responses to AI differ across contexts. It identifies career resilience, AI self-efficacy, learning ability, training, supportive leadership, organisational support, employee participation, transparency, and human-centred AI governance as important potential buffers. A qualitative thematic synthesis is used because the included studies differ substantially in constructs, occupational settings, countries, research designs, and outcome measures. The review does not claim exhaustive coverage of proprietary bibliographic databases such as Scopus or Web of Science. No new human-participant data were collected. This work is released as a research preprint for open scholarly dissemination and future updating as additional database records become available.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Utility in India by 2047
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence may become an ordinary input into economic and civic life, accessed through services as routinely as electricity. This essay examines what that possibility means for India as it approaches the centenary of independence in 2047. Building on the argument of The Grid That Thinks, it uses the history of electrification and selected research on productivity, AI costs and infrastructure to assess the utility analogy. The central argument is that affordable computational capability produces broad social value only when institutions reorganise around it and access includes language, reliability, accountability and effective redress. The analogy illuminates complementary investment and unequal diffusion, but weakens when applied to the measurement of intelligence, market structure and systems that interpret information or act on users' behalf. The essay proposes a plural infrastructure approach combining shared public capabilities, competing providers, local evaluation and human fallback. items.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Utility in India by 2047
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence may become an ordinary input into economic and civic life, accessed through services as routinely as electricity. This essay examines what that possibility means for India as it approaches the centenary of independence in 2047. Building on the argument of The Grid That Thinks, it uses the history of electrification and selected research on productivity, AI costs and infrastructure to assess the utility analogy. The central argument is that affordable computational capability produces broad social value only when institutions reorganise around it and access includes language, reliability, accountability and effective redress. The analogy illuminates complementary investment and unequal diffusion, but weakens when applied to the measurement of intelligence, market structure and systems that interpret information or act on users' behalf. The essay proposes a plural infrastructure approach combining shared public capabilities, competing providers, local evaluation and human fallback. It treats 2047 as a planning horizon rather than a forecast and identifies observable outcomes by which the promise of an intelligence utility could be judged.

items.title: Artificial intelligence as enabler and object of strategic foresight: a theoretical framework for digital organisational transformation
items.abstract: Purpose Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in organisations has concentrated on operational efficiency and automation. This study aims to reposition AI as both a constitutive element and a strategic object of foresight, a dual role the literature has noticed but not theorised. Design/methodology/approach A narrative literature review draws peer-reviewed work from foresight studies, socio-technical systems theory and organisational change into an integrated analytical framework. Selection prioritised conceptual contribution, transparency of reasoning and relevance to AI in strategic futures thinking. Findings AI strengthens environmental sensing, complex modelling and scenario work under uncertainty. The framework has four components: inputs, AI systems, human–AI interaction and outcomes, and yields five propositions for empirical testing. Research limitations/implications As a theoretical contribution, empirical validation remains a priority. Findings should be tested across sectors and organisational contexts before generalisation. Practical implications Organisations must cultivate digital foresight literacy, restructure around cross-functional foresight teams and implement agile governance capable of auditing AI-generated outputs. The framework provides guidance for navigating algorithmic bias, transparency obligations and power asymmetries. Originality/value This study makes four contributions. It reconceptualises AI as constitutive of organisational foresight instead of an instrument applied to it, introduces and differentiates anticipatory co-evolution as a novel construct, integrates Rohrbeck’s (2010) maturity model with Ivanov’s (2023) configuration taxonomy and sets out ethical governance requirements specific to AI-enabled foresight.
