items.title: Artificial Intelligence Coaching for Confident Speaking and Spontaneous Argumentation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support spoken language practice. However, different AI-assisted support systems do not support learners’ confidence equally. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examines associations among the perceived usefulness of AI feedback, AI-mediated argumentative scaffolding, self-reported cognitive engagement, and speaking self-efficacy in the context of spontaneous argumentation. The quantitative phase involved 130 university EFL learners who had used an AI-assisted argumentation coaching application for at least eight weeks. Regression analysis showed that perceived usefulness of AI feedback was positively associated with so-called speaking self-efficacy, that is, the confidence to perform spoken tasks successfully (β = .410, p < .001), as was AI-mediated argumentative scaffolding (β = .248, p = .002). In contrast, self-reported cognitive engagement was not significantly associated with speaking self-efficacy after the other predictors were taken into account (β = −.028, p = .725). The qualitative phase involved eight purposively selected participants representing variation in gender, year of study, IELTS target, and experiences relevant to the quantitative patterns. Thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews identified three explanatory themes: structural scaffolding, psychological safety, and cognitive limits. Participants frequently described organizational guidance and a nonjudgmental practice environment as useful, while some also reported repetition, fatigue, and dependence during extended AI use. Integrating the two phases suggests that perceived usefulness, scaffolding, and cognitive engagement should not be treated as interchangeable dimensions of AI-assisted speaking practice. The study proposes a provisional cognitive-threshold hypothesis for future testing, but does not claim a causal or nonlinear effect. The findings support strategically designed AI-assisted speaking practice that maintains opportunities for independent reasoning and human interaction.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education and Research: Transforming Teaching and Learning in Economics
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in education and research, fundamentally reshaping teaching methodologies, learning experiences, and knowledge production in economics. This paper examines the role of AI in enhancing pedagogical practices, improving research efficiency, and redefining skill requirements in economics education. Drawing on recent empirical and theoretical literature, the study highlights key applications such as personalised learning, intelligent tutoring systems, data-driven research tools, and automated assessment. It also evaluates critical challenges including ethical concerns, academic integrity, digital inequality, and overreliance on AI systems. Empirically, the study utilised annual time series data from 2010 to 2024 and adopted the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model to analyse both short-run and long-run dynamics. Findings show that AI has a positive and statistically significant effect on learning outcomes in both the short run and long run. The paper concludes that while AI offers substantial opportunities for innovation in economics education and research, its successful integration requires strategic policy frameworks, ethical guidelines, and capacity building among educators and students.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND CLINICAL PRACTICE: A NARRATIVE REVIEW
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping medicine, influencing clinicians’ training and patient care. Despite growing enthusiasm for AI-enabled diagnostics and digital learning tools, integration of these technologies into medical education and clinical practice remains uneven. Objective: This narrative review synthesises recent literature on the role of AI in medical education and clinical practice, mapping current applications, stakeholder perceptions, and the conditions that determine successful adoption. Methods: Relevant articles were identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, and EMBASE, prioritising literature from the last decade. Empirical studies, methodological reviews, and authoritative commentaries addressing AI, machine learning, or digital health technologies in clinical or educational settings were included and organised thematically. Findings: AI-powered tools are embedded across medical training, spanning augmented and virtual reality simulations, bedside mobile learning, and a range of clinical specialties, with performance matching expert levels on narrowly defined diagnostic tasks. Stakeholder attitudes are positive but conditional: medical students expect digital health technology to feature in their curricula yet many consider their own competencies inadequate, and very few physicians-in-training report familiarity with AI. Patients express willingness to engage with AI for self-management while preferring human contact in sensitive clinical domains. Persistent barriers remain, including limited availability of curated data, algorithmic bias, difficulties reproducing published models, and underdeveloped regulatory and workflow structures. Conclusion: AI delivers its greatest value when deployed as a collaborative instrument that augments rather than replaces clinical judgment. Realising this potential depends on sustained investment in digital literacy, explainable systems, clinician involvement in design, and equitable institutional infrastructure.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in risk-based auditing of large enterprise taxation
items.abstract: The article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations for applying artificial intelligence (AI) in risk-based audits of large enterprise taxation. The study’s relevance stems from the significant fiscal role of large taxpayers, the complexity of their business transactions, the prevalence of cross-border transactions and transfer pricing practices, and the need to identify tax risks promptly amid the digital transformation of tax administration. The study aims to identify areas for AI application to improve the effectiveness of identifying, assessing, and prioritizing tax risks for large enterprises. Based on an analysis of academic research and international approaches, the study systematizes the key tax risks inherent in large enterprises, including those related to transfer pricing, profit shifting across jurisdictions, transactions involving intangible assets, intra-group financing, corporate income taxation, value-added tax (VAT), and tax compliance. The study explores the potential of machine learning, anomaly detection algorithms, predictive analytics, natural language processing (NLP), cluster analysis, and network analysis for processing large volumes of financial and tax data. This study develops a structural and logical model for applying AI in risk-based audits of large enterprise taxation, integrating information and analytical support, AI tools, tax risk profiling, and the auditor’s professional judgment. AI-driven analysis should provide an analytical basis for identifying areas of heightened tax risk and prioritizing audit procedures, while final audit decisions should remain grounded in the auditor’s professional judgment. The practical significance of the findings lies in the potential application of the proposed approach to enhance the validity and effectiveness of risk-based audits of large enterprise taxation. Keywords: artificial intelligence, risk-based audit, tax audit, large enterprises, tax risks, transfer pricing, machine learning, tax compliance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Traditional Medical Systems: Emerging Ethical and Governance Challenges for Health Systems
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into traditional medical systems such as Ayurveda and Traditional Chinese Medicine is expanding rapidly, with applications in diagnosis, treatment planning, and decision support. While these developments may improve access and efficiency, they introduce important challenges for healthcare systems, particularly in relation to data quality, clinical validity, regulatory oversight, and practitioner reliance on algorithmic tools. Current governance frameworks largely overlook AI applications in traditional medicine, creating gaps in accountability and quality assurance. This letter highlights key system-level concerns and emphasizes the need for context-specific validation, regulatory clarity, and interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure the safe and effective integration of AI within traditional healthcare practices.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy in Slavonic Studies: Student Reflections
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence literacy is usually assessed through self-report scales. Such instruments show where a group stands, but not how its members reason about the technology in their own terms. Research on this topic has also concentrated on science and technology disciplines and on high-resource languages. It remains unclear how students working in low-resource languages, such as the Slavonic languages, articulate their artificial intelligence literacy, and what knowledge underlies their evaluative judgments. This study analyses written reflections and a background questionnaire from students of Slavonic studies, translation and language teaching who completed a one-semester course in artificial intelligence literacy. The reflections were produced after students used a generative artificial intelligence tool as both the commissioner and the collaborator of an individual academic project. They were examined through qualitative content analysis combining deductive and inductive categories. The findings show that the reflections centre overwhelmingly on evaluating outputs, while declarative knowledge of how such systems function remains a knowledge of symptoms rather than of mechanisms. Evaluative judgments depend heavily on disciplinary expertise in areas such as phonetics, lexicology, translation and language pedagogy, rather than on general critical thinking, and target precisely the errors a domain-uninformed reader would not detect. The questionnaire further shows that students already held a critical disposition toward artificial intelligence before the course began, which constrains how the reflective practice documented here can be interpreted. Taken together, the results reposition disciplinary expertise, more than technical understanding of artificial intelligence, as the primary resource for critical evaluation, with direct implications for teaching artificial intelligence literacy and language technology in higher education.

items.title: Atomic‐Layer Materials for Energy Storage Systems
items.abstract: Atomic-layer materials (ALMs) provide a promising platform for electrochemical energy storage because their atomically thin structures and interfaces enable control over ion adsorption, charge transfer, diffusion pathways, and interfacial stability. In this review, ALMs include both intrinsic two-dimensional (2D) materials and atomic-layer-engineered functional coatings and interphases produced by atomic layer deposition (ALD), molecular layer deposition (MLD), or related approaches. This work connects atomic-scale design variables, including atomic-scale structural parameters, with device-level performance, degradation, and manufacturability. Their sustainability in batteries and supercapacitors (SCs) will be the main focus. Particular attention is given to how these variables regulate interfacial electrochemical phenomena, metal-ion deposition, and mechanical stability. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are discussed as ALM-specific tools for screening and optimizing ALD/MLD coating chemistry and deposition conditions. Although ALMs offer advantages in laboratory results, practical deployment remains limited by techno-economic bottlenecks or industrial scalability barriers for 2D material processing and device integration. Near-term commercialization is promising for high-leverage interfacial-modification functions in batteries and integrated micro-energy-storage devices. This review also provides a manufacturing framework for discussing the development of durable, scalable, and AI-enabled ALM-based energy-storage technologies.

items.title: Between Determinism and Chance: From Llull's Machine to Generative AI Models
items.abstract: In 1937, Jorge Luis Borges looked back some 650 years at Ramon Llull‘s machinic ars inveniendi. This is one of five essays that looks at contemporary learning machines through the lens of Borges‘s characteristically engimatic historical note and literary reflection. It examines the epistemological tension between determinism and randomness in projects of formalising thought – from Ramon Llull's Ars Magna (1305) to contemporary generative transformers. Borges's 1937 critique of Llull revealed a fundamental impasse: closed combinatorial systems, lacking contextual sensitivity, produce syntactic noise rather than truth. Yet Borges proposed an alternative, namely, to use such machines as generators of random combinations subject to human selection. This shift finds unexpected validation in AI transformer models. By replacing discrete symbols with continuous semantic embeddings and dynamic attention mechanisms, transformers overcome Llull's linear blindness. However, in deterministic mode (low temperature), they merely reproduce linguistic clichés, exhibiting neural text degeneration. Genuine novelty emerges only through stochastic sampling–temperature-based deviation into the probability distribution's long tail, actualising latent semantic projections (as in the Borgesian “red tiger”). Drawing on recent empirical studies, the paper demonstrates a fundamental trade-off between alignment due to reinforcement learning (RLHF) and stochastic creativity. As an alternative, calibrated uncertainty is proposed, allowing models to acknowledge the limits of knowledge. The transformer that legitimises its stochastic nature thereby approaches Borges's ideal of a poetic machine – an instrument that does not prove but suggests, that does not close off truth but opens a space for play.

items.title: Beyond the algorithm
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly integrated into occupational health medicine practice, offering potential improvements in diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. However, their implementation introduces novel challenges, including algorithmic bias, lack of transparency in decision-making processes, and risks of over-reliance on automated outputs without appropriate clinical judgment. As occupational health decisions directly affect both individual worker protection and broader workplace public health, professionals must develop advanced information literacy that extends beyond traditional source evaluation to include a critical understanding of AI systems themselves, including their underlying data sources, technical limitations, and potential biases. This study evaluated AI information literacy among 16 occupational health professionals (specialists and residents) participating in the EASOM Summer School 2025. A five-item knowledge-based assessment adapted to occupational health contexts evaluated participants' competencies in identifying biased research questions, selecting evidence retrieval strategies, assessing the accuracy of AI-generated content, applying ethical AI use practices, and understanding proper citation protocols. Overall mean quiz performance was 2.56/5 points (SD = 1.09), indicating substantial gaps in AI information literacy. Questions assessing biased research design yielded the poorest performance (12.5% correct), while questions on ethical AI use in academia (81.2% correct) and citation practices (68.8% correct) demonstrated higher competency. Age showed significant negative correlation with quiz scores (ρ = −0.511, p = 0.043), suggesting younger professionals are better prepared for AI-integrated practice. These findings, although comprised from a small sample, demonstrate the need for targeted educational interventions addressing algorithmic bias recognition, critical question formulation, and responsible AI integration in occupational health medicine practice and worker protection.

items.title: Bridging the Digital Learning Divide: Artificial Intelligence, Access, and the Social Determinants of Higher Education Outcomes in Africa
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence into African higher education has renewed the expectation that technology will close long-standing gaps in educational opportunity. This study argues that the expectation will be disappointed unless the digital learning divide is understood as a socially structured condition, and not merely as a question of who owns a device or holds a connection. The study adopts a conceptual-analytical design based on theoretical adaptation and synthesis rather than primary data. Sources were selected purposively from the sociology of the digital divide, the social determinants of health framework, and fundamental cause theory. Constructs were retained only where the valued outcome is influenced by flexible resources and the mechanisms producing it change over time, and were then applied to artificial intelligence in African higher education using recent continental connectivity evidence. The analysis yields a three-tier social determinants model of higher education outcomes, in which structural determinants, intermediary determinants, and differential digital access, use and outcome operate together, bound by flexible resources that generate cumulative advantage. Within this model, artificial intelligence amplifies opportunity where infrastructure, preparation, support and governance are present, and amplifies disadvantage where they are absent. Interventions confined to access are therefore absorbed without disturbing the achievement gradient, and average effects can conceal a widening distributional gap. Governments and institutions should fund the enabling conditions as components of any artificial intelligence programme; target the achievement gradient through proportionate universalism; subject classifying systems to equity audit, explanation, contestation and data protection; and ground platforms in local context, language and participation. Bridging the digital learning divide is a task of social redistribution, not only of technological supply. Keywords: digital access; digital skills; artificial intelligence adoption; socioeconomic status; higher education outcomes; educational equity

items.title: Claiming sociodigital futures? Knowledge practices and their consequences
items.abstract: There is currently intense and widespread speculation about the implications of digital technologies for future societies, despite a wealth of evidence that past claims to predict how technology will shape the future have usually failed. Nonetheless, it is now well established that claims to knowledge about how emerging technologies will shape future worlds are performative, exercising powerful effects on the futures they claim to describe. Building on the Sociology of Expectations and work on Sociotechnical Imaginaries, this paper turns attention to the ontological and epistemological ‘nuts’ and ‘bolts’ of claims about digital technologies, social life and the future. We ask: how are these entities and the relations between them constituted and given traction as knowledge practices? Specifically, we explore the practices used by major future-claiming institutional actors in a selection of published documents. We find a strikingly coherent ontological performance of the relations between ‘the digital’, ‘the social’ and ‘the future’ and the circulation of (what comes to count as) knowledge across these institutions. Indeed, what is striking is the re-purposability of these knowledge practices despite the distinctive institutional interests in play. These knowledge practices offer a limited grasp on the futures that are currently in the making. Moreover, they enable the persistence of a latent set of assumptions which are powerful in limiting consideration of critical questions about the future.

items.title: Cognitive Capabilities of the Interface in Machine Learning: A Philosophical Perspective
items.abstract: The actual problems of digital technology in the machine learning field are related to the expansion of autonomous intelligent systems in respect to cognitive activity. The growth in the volume of information in modern networks requires new formats for working with knowledge, based on hybrid systems and neural models of artificial intelligence (AI). Neural network training involves the formation of experience of semantic orientations in multi-valued contexts using self-correction mechanisms. In the modeling of virtual machine learning environments, the role of the interface increases. The article examines the cognitive potential of the interface as a factor shaping the boundaries and modes of functional autonomy of artificial intelligence systems in machine learning. The interface is treated not as a neutral technical channel of information transfer but as a semantic matrix that programs a sequence of cognitive operations – selection, context-binding, inference, revision, and action. Particular attention is given to the temporal dimension of the interface's cognitive potential. The authors introduce the concept of chronotope (Mikhail Bakhtin) as a model for organizing the interplay of space and time within the virtual learning environment, and analyze temporal event models grounded in metaphors, image schemas, and grammatical constructions. The communicative design of the interface is discussed through the lens of cultural archetypes (Carl Gustav Jung), which shape “trusted agent” models in human–AI dialogue. Factors determining the interface's cognitive function – structuring the space of relevant information, temporal dynamics, inference formation, optimization regimes, and actor motivation – are systematized. The authors conclude that the interface's cognitive potential establishes the conditions for the subject's semantic orientation and the digital agent's goal-directed behavior, ensuring the coupling of human and artificial intelligence in the expanded production of knowledge.

items.title: Conceptualising Organisational Organic Cognition: A Fifth Dimension of organisational kinetics
items.abstract: Abstract Organisations constantly find themselves in a dynamic environment, where technology is disrupting and influencing their way of working, artificial intelligence and automation is being adopted, market segments are volatile and rapidly growing, regulators are ever evolving and complex, and stakeholders have rapidly changing expectations. Theories of organisational change such as dynamic capabilities, organisational cognition, absorptive capacity and organisational learning, offer comprehensive explanations as to how organisations react to change. These views, however, offer insufficient understanding of the cognitive process by which a group of people collectively make sense of what changes in the environment mean and how appropriate action should be taken. This study therefore builds on the organisational change phenomenon with a mindset of organisational organic cognition as a fifth dimension of organisational kinetics. The study argued that organisational organic cognition is viewed as an organisation-wide capacity of sensing, interpreting, learning and adapting to constantly evolving environment and convert experiences into knowledge and respond timely to achieve organisational goal. The study concludes that organisational organic cognition relates with organisational kinetics as a mechanism that connects organisational information, organisational choices and organisational adaptation. Keywords: Organisational Organic Cognition, Organisational Kinetics, organisational agility, organisational learning, sensemaking

items.title: Conocer a Picasso en Educación Primaria a través de la Gamificación e Inteligencia Artificial Generativa
items.abstract: In recent years, the integration of innovative methodologies, such as gamification and generative artificial intelligence (AI), has opened up new possibilities in art education. This study examines the impact of a gamified intervention incorporating AI-based activities on the creative development of primary school students, evaluating its effectiveness in enhancing artistic and narrative expression. A quasi-experimental single-group design with pre- and post-intervention measures was implemented using the Prueba de Imaginación Creativa – Niños (PIC-N). The intervention was structured around a gamified narrative, in which students assumed the role of artistic explorers tasked with rescuing Picasso. The findings reveal a significant increase in both graphic and narrative creativity, accompanied by enhanced fluency, flexibility, and originality. Moreover, no gender differences were found, indicating that the intervention had an equitable impact. The results reinforce the effectiveness of gamification and generative AI as strategies to enhance creativity in the classroom. The importance of avoiding pointsification and promoting meaningful experiences is emphasized. Despite the benefits, several challenges were identified, including the risk of technological dependence and the need to strike a balance between digital experimentation and the development of manual skills.

items.title: Covert Systems – On the Intelligence of Large Language Models
items.abstract: In light of recent developments in Artificial Intelligence, particularly the development of Large Language Models (LLMs), the question if machines can be said to think is examined. The problem was already addressed by Alan Turing in the 1950s, laying the groundwork for our argumentation. Our text refutes four common objections. Firstly, it challenges Ada Lovelace’s claim that computers are incapable of creating truly original content, demonstrating that neural networks, such as Transformer models, independently generate novel structures. Secondly, the assertion that LLMs merely statistically predict the next word is discussed. They are shown to be capable of constructing compressed internal representations from their input data through nonlinear operations, distinguishing them from statistical models. A third argument concerns AI’s lack of sensory access to the world. However, as Turing has demonstrated, the development of mental capabilities requires only communication between a teacher and a student, and sensory experience can be technically replicated at any time. The Chinese Room thought experiment, which suggests that algorithms merely simulate intelligence through formal symbol manipulation, is already anticipated by the Turing Test, which posits that any machine successfully feigning mental functions should be deemed to possess them. The text explores how LLMs generate a perfect compression of their input data, resulting in an accurate model of the world, a convincing simulation of human intelligence, and mastery of language. It discusses the phenomenon of “emergence”, the appearance of higher-order cognitive capabilities with increasing amounts of training data. Although the successes in implementing intelligence are notable, the neural network methodology employed results in the enigmaticity of the underlying basis, failing to illuminate the true nature of the mind as originally hoped. This obscurity was already evident in the foundational works of Kurt Gödel and Alan Turing, highlighting the complexities inherent in understanding human and machine intelligence alike.

items.title: Crafting the future of drinks: a TAM and Jd-R perspective on bartenders’ AI adoption
items.abstract: As AI transforms hospitality, its role in creative areas like bartending is underexplored. This study uses the Technology Acceptance Model and Job Demands-Resources theory to examine bartenders’ adoption of AI tools for drink creation. A survey of 384 U.S. bartenders analyzed the impact of ease of use, usefulness, job demands, and resources on AI attitudes, job strain, motivation, and turnover. Results from Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) indicate that both TAM variables significantly shape attitudes toward AI, while job demands increase strain and reduce retention. Although job resources reduce strain, they do not significantly enhance motivation. Additionally, positive AI attitudes and intrinsic motivation reduce turnover intentions, while job strain increases them. Findings extend theory and offer insights for encouraging AI adoption and staff retention.

items.title: CREDIT BY ALGORITHM: REGULATING DIGITAL LENDING IN INDIA
items.abstract: The Reserve Bank of India (Digital Lending) Directions, 2025 define digital lending as a remote and largelyautomated process running through six stages, from customer acquisition to recovery. One of those stagesis credit assessment. It is the only area that the Directions leave unregulated.Every operative obligation in the Directions attaches to what surrounds the assessment rather than to theassessment itself: the Key Fact Statement and the annualized rate, disbursal into the borrower’s ownaccount, the cooling-off period, the conduct of recovery, grievance redressal, and the public directory oflending applications. An applicant refused credit by a model receives none of it.The regulator is not unaware. Its own Committee on a Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablementof Artificial Intelligence reported in August 2025 that regulated entities already deploy artificialintelligence in credit underwriting, and recommended disclosure of its use together with a human right ofoverride. That report is advisory. It binds nobody.This article argues that the resulting gap is regulatory rather than legislative. The Reserve Bank alreadypossesses the power it would need, and has exercised that power comprehensively at every stage of adigital loan except the stage that decides whether the loan is made at all. The argument is tested againstthe Directions, the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005 and the applicant’s existing rightof access to credit information, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the standard ofproportionality applied to Reserve Bank regulation in Internet and Mobile Association of India v. ReserveBank of India. It concludes that assessment can be brought within the framework by direction, withoutamendment to any statute.

items.title: Developing AI‐driven decision support for the proactive identification and evaluation of financially distressed companies by Belgian commercial courts
items.abstract: Abstract The early identification and accurate evaluation of financially distressed companies by commercial courts is crucial for maintaining a healthy economic fabric. This enables timely support for struggling companies with recovery potential while also facilitating the swift winding up of those unlikely to recover. Despite its economic importance, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in this context remains limited. We investigate how an AI‐based decision support system can be designed and validated to support commercial court judges in identifying and evaluating financially distressed companies. Specifically, we train predictive machine learning models that combine red flag data (e.g., social security debt, debt under seizure) with annual account data to predict whether a company will be referred for bankruptcy proceedings and to rank companies by their likelihood of referral to enable prioritization. Results indicate moderately strong performance, underscoring the potential of AI‐assisted decision‐making. Importantly, the proposed system does not replace judges, but supports them in allocating scarce resources more effectively.

items.title: Digital Barbarism and the Self-deregulation of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: In late 2026, the institutional landscape surrounding artificial intelligence reached a critical turning point as public warnings of existential risk intersected with major cybersecurity incidents, corporate resignations, and federal self-regulation frameworks. This paper evaluates the political economy of frontier AI governance by analyzing the rhetoric of "pacing" development and the voluntary "White House Accord on Super Intelligence" (Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities). I argue that corporate calls for safety pacing operate as an ideological mechanism that replaces democratic public oversight with closed, profit-driven corporate self-surveillance while shielding firms from legal liability. By framing technical software execution failures as evidence of autonomous superintelligence, tech elites legitimize market enclosure and top-down administrative control. Finally, the paper proposes democratic technoskepticism as an alternative framework that reclaims computing power, data infrastructure, and algorithmic knowledge as digital commons subject to direct democratic governance.

items.title: Digital Ethnobotany: Artificial Intelligence, GIS and Mobile Technologies for Traditional Knowledge Documentation
items.abstract: Ethnobotanical knowledge represents an important component of biocultural heritage, which includes traditional relationships between people and plants for medicinal, nutritional, cultural, ecological and economic purposes. Much of this knowledge is transmitted orally and remains vulnerable to cultural transformation, environmental degradation, loss of traditional languages and weakening intergenerational transmission. The present study attempts to review digital ethnobotany and use of emerging digital and Artificial Intelligence tools for documenting traditional knowledge. Digital ethnobotany has emerged as an interdisciplinary approach that integrates conventional ethnobotanical methods with digital databases, artificial intelligence (AI), Geographic Information Systems (GIS), mobile technologies, digital repositories and multimedia platforms. These technologies provide new opportunities for systematic documentation, preservation, organization, analysis and dissemination of traditional and Indigenous plant knowledge. AI can support image-based plant identification, machine learning, Natural Language Processing (NLP) and computational analysis of ethnobotanical datasets, whereas GIS and GeoAI facilitate spatial analysis of plant resources, traditional-use patterns and plant, people and environment relationships. Mobile technologies enable real-time field documentation through smartphones, GPS, digital questionnaires, geotagged photographs, audio-video recording and plant-identification applications, including fieldwork in remote areas through offline data collection. Digital databases and digitized collections further facilitate the integration of taxonomic, ecological, cultural, geographical and ethnopharmacological information. However, technological applications are associated with challenges including taxonomic errors, data-quality limitations, algorithmic bias, digital inequality, privacy risks, loss of cultural context and unauthorized access or commercialization of traditional knowledge. Ethical safeguards including prior informed consent, community participation, intellectual-property protection, Indigenous data governance, controlled access and expert validation are therefore essential. The future of digital ethnobotany lies in a symbiotic AI community model in which digital technologies complement, rather than replace, botanical expertise and the knowledge of local and Indigenous communities.

items.title: Digitalization of marketing and logistics processes in the e-commerce system
items.abstract: The article investigates the role of digitalization of marketing and logistics processes in the e-commerce system as a key factor in enhancing the competitiveness of modern enterprises. The central industry problem is the lack of synergy between marketing strategies and logistics operations, described as fragmented or “patchwork” digitalization, where sales channels remain unsynchronized with supply chains, reducing overall service efficiency and undermining enterprise competitiveness. The relevance of this research is further confirmed at the regulatory level by the Law of Ukraine “On Electronic Commerce,” which sets requirements for business entities’ digital infrastructure and directly requires a systemic approach to digitalizing marketing and logistics processes. The study demonstrates that the global e-commerce market exceeded 6.3 trillion USD in 2024, with online sales accounting for 20.1% of global retail turnover. The Ukrainian market recorded a 25% increase in online sales in 2024, reaching 239 billion hryvnias, with 11 million active online shoppers. At the same time, e-commerce accounts for only 10% of Ukrainian retail, half the level in Poland, indicating significant unrealized potential. Key challenges facing enterprises include cybersecurity threats, intensifying competition, rising advertising costs, uneven geographic distribution of online trade, and regulatory uncertainty under martial law conditions. In the domain of marketing transformation, the article examines omnichannel strategy as a synchronization of all communication flows into a single customer-oriented system. The article analyzes personalization as the primary objective of omnichannel implementation, achieved through Big Data, artificial intelligence, and interactive content, enabling individual customer scenarios ranging from product recommendations to dynamic pricing. CRM systems fall into four functional groups: operational, analytical, collaborative, and combined. They function as a unified information hub that aggregates customer data from all interaction channels and serves as a primary source for precision advertising targeting. Big Data is presented as the technological foundation enabling comprehensive consumer profiling that extends beyond traditional demographics to include psychographic parameters and digital activity patterns, with machine learning algorithms underpinning predictive analytics. Behavioral targeting relies on dynamic user activity indicators such as session duration, content browsing depth, and incomplete transactions, with precision targeting identified as a baseline condition for marketing budget profitability amid rising traffic costs. In the logistics dimension, the article analyzes automated warehouse management incorporating robotized order picking, RFID identification, and IoT-based real-time inventory monitoring. According to McKinsey estimates, generative AI in warehouse logistics reduces administrative workload by 10–20% and documentation preparation time by up to 60%. The global AI market in logistics was valued at 20.1 billion USD in 2024 and is projected to grow at 25.9% annually through 2034. AI solutions in supply chains reduce logistics costs by 15% and inventory volumes by 35%. Last-mile delivery accounts for 41% of total logistics expenditure on average, with its market valued at 161.2 billion USD in 2024 and projected to reach 373.9 billion USD by 2033. Micro-fulfillment centers are examined as automated urban warehouses enabling same-day delivery without an extensive proprietary logistics network. The article’s principal contribution is a three-level conceptual model for integrating marketing and logistics processes. The first level, data integration, involves building a unified data lake that consolidates marketing, logistics, and CRM data to enable demand forecasting. The second level, real-time process synchronization, ensures marketing decisions automatically translate into logistics responses, including excluding high-defect products from campaigns based on return data. The third level, customer journey personalization accounting for logistics capabilities, links recommendation systems to inventory management to prevent post-purchase disappointment. Research confirms that such omnichannel integration delivers cost savings of approximately 13% compared to the traditional sequential approach. Future research could include empirical testing of the model with specific companies and an examination of autonomous distribution systems and micro-fulfillment centers in the context of post-war reconstruction in Ukrainian e-commerce. Keywords: digitalization, e-commerce, marketing and logistics processes, digital marketing, logistics, Big Data, artificial intelligence, CRM systems, omnichannel strategies.

items.title: Direct and multi-level machine translation: Korean-Uzbek and Korean-English-Uzbek language pairs
items.abstract: This pilot study compares direct Korean–Uzbek machine translation with a pivot-based Korean–English–Uzbek workflow for a low-resource language pair. Two Korean public-information texts, divided into ten long segments, were translated using Google Translate and ChatGPT. The outputs were examined manually using selected Multidimensional Quality Metrics categories accuracy, fluency and style and were then compared using the automatic metric BLEU. Manual annotation identified fifteen errors in the direct output and four errors in the pivot-based output. However, the reported BLEU scores were higher for the direct workflow in both texts (41.21 versus 22.98; 46.53 versus 8.91). Manual and automatic evaluation therefore produced opposite rankings. The discrepancy shows that surface n-gram overlap and human judgments of meaning and naturalness measure different aspects of translation quality, and that a single metric is insufficient for this language pair. Because the dataset is small and the evaluation settings are incompletely documented, the findings are exploratory rather than generalizable.
